amendments.rule: A genitive name of relationship takes the whole English expression the ASV builds around it, including the relational noun the ASV supplies, as one `aligned` unit headed on the name. `Ἰούδα Σίμωνος Ἰσκαριώτου` → *of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son* gives *Simon's son* to `Σίμωνος` headed on *Simon's*, and the same construction at John 13:26 and John 6:71 → *the son of Simon Iscariot* gives the whole *the son of* to that word headed on *Simon*. No Greek token answers to *son*: the bare genitive is all that carries the relation, so the supplied noun and its determiner are rule 7 helpers on the name and rule 11 keeps the ASV's italics from making them `added`. Rule 17 then holds the head on the name rather than on the supplied generic noun, exactly as it does for `ταῦτα` → *these things*, and the case preposition *of* rides along as it does for any source noun rendered `of + noun`. Which of the two phrasings the ASV chooses changes nothing, which is rule 24's habit. Rule 20 is not the contrast: there the Greek expresses the head noun, as `ὁ θρόνος τοῦ Σατανᾶ` → *Satan's throne* does, and the genitive name only displaces the article's determiner, whereas here no head noun is expressed and the genitive is the only word the supplied one can belong to. That last clause is this rule's whole scope and is to be read strictly, because an **article** is also a word a supplied noun can belong to: this rule reaches an **anarthrous** genitive alone. Where an article stands in front of the genitive and no head noun is expressed — the `τοῦ` of a genealogical link — rule 102 takes the supplied noun into that article's own phrase instead and this rule does not apply: the article takes the supplied nominal together with its determiner and the case preposition, headed on the supplied nominal, and the genitive name stands bare. `τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ τοῦ Ἠλί` → *the son of Joseph, the son of Heli* gives *the son of* to each article, headed on *son*, and a bare *Joseph* and *Heli* to the names, as LUK.3.23–38 reads its whole genealogy, and as the chain's closing `τοῦ θεοῦ` → *the son of God* reads a member that is a noun rather than a name. Rule 102's own test is what decides it, and it is the test rules 51 and 58 already use — whether a Greek article stands to take the determiner — so the presence of the article and not the shape of the English is what chooses between the two readings: a link the Greek writes **anarthrously** and the ASV still renders *the son of* is this rule's case and takes the expression whole, as `Ἰούδας Ἰακώβου` → *Judas the son of James* does. Do not split the supplied *son* from its determiner or from the case preposition, and do not mark a repeated one `added`: rule 103 folds a supplied nominal standing inside a phrase a Greek article governs into that article's own English however plainly it echoes a noun the same verse or the neighbouring verse expresses.
amendments.why: Rule 52's closing sentence — that where no head noun is expressed 'the genitive is the only word the supplied one can belong to' — is over-broad, and LUK.3 is the case it had not considered: 76 genealogical links of `τοῦ` + name where the ASV supplies *the son of* and an article does stand to take it. Rule 102 already decides those correctly (an article takes a supplied determiner plus nominal, headed on the nominal, 53 corpus units to none), so the fault is that a reader meeting `τοῦ Ἰωσήφ` reads rule 52 first and is told the name takes the whole expression. Amending 52 corrects the sentence where it stands rather than leaving it in place behind a cross-reference. Nothing in the corpus contradicts the narrowing: every example rule 52 itself cites is anarthrous (`Σίμωνος` at JHN.13.26 and JHN.6.71), so the amendment removes no attested case from the rule. The construction recurs well beyond this chapter — `Ἰούδας Ἰακώβου`, `Μαρία ἡ τοῦ Κλωπᾶ`, `Ἰάκωβος ὁ τοῦ Ζεβεδαίου` — which is why the articular/anarthrous test is stated as the decider. I deliberately said nothing about the double-article shape (`ὁ τοῦ Ζεβεδαίου`), which LUK.3 does not contain and which I have no corpus evidence for.

conventions: Genealogy, 3.23-3.38: each `τοῦ` + name link is split under rule 102 - the article takes the supplied *son* together with its determiner and the case *of*, headed on *son*, and the name stands bare. Rule 52's whole-expression-on-the-name reading was declined because an article stands here to take the supplied nominal, and rule 103 does not make the repeated *son* `added`, the article's own phrase being incomplete without it. The chain's last link, `τοῦ θεοῦ` at 3.38, is read identically though its member is a noun and not a name.

An English preposition standing over an accusative object stays inside the verb's unit throughout the chapter, under rule 106's accusative arm: `μηδένα διασείσητε` -> *Extort from no man by violence* at 3.14 keeps *from*, and `εὐηγγελίζετο τὸν λαόν` -> *preached he good tidings unto the people* at 3.18 keeps *unto*, the article taking only *the* and the noun standing bare. Giving *unto the* to the article under rule 21 is the competing reading and was declined because an accusative has no case for an English preposition to realize. A dative or genitive object is the contrast and keeps its own case preposition, as `τῷ Ἀβραάμ` -> *unto Abraham* does at 3.8.

Two form-ambiguous articles are read under rule 57 as governing their head noun across an interposed genitive rather than as standing before the name that follows them: `τῆς Ἰτουραίας καὶ Τραχωνίτιδος χώρας` at 3.1 gives *of the* to `τῆς` and leaves `χώρας` bare, and `τὸν Ζαχαρίου υἱόν` at 3.2 gives *the* to `τόν` and leaves `υἱόν` bare. The three province articles of 3.1 (`τῆς Ἰουδαίας`, `τῆς Γαλιλαίας`, `τῆς Ἀβιληνῆς`) are the contrast: no determiner is written for their nouns, so they are `unrepresented` under rule 21's determinerless clause and each *of* stays with its noun.

report: Read all 46 candidate groups and the full dump end to end. No cross-verse split found; patches empty.

The large `ὁ` group resolves into five uniformly applied regimes: `the` where the ASV writes a determiner; `unrepresented` for want of one (rule 21's determinerless clause at 3.1 s012/s016/s032, 3.6 s007, 3.8 s005) or because a possessive or demonstrative took the slot (3.4, 3.8 s025, 3.14, 3.15, 3.17, 3.19, 3.22); the bare pronoun before a participle or adjective (3.11, 3.13, 3.16 s013); rule 57 across an interposed genitive (3.1 s025, 3.2 s011); and rule 102's `the son of` through 3.23-3.38. Each is licensed by its own configuration.

`καί` unrepresented at 3.18 against *also* elsewhere, and `μέν` unrepresented at 3.18 against *indeed* at 3.16, are rules 65 and 70's English-side test, not two analyses. The two `εἰς` of 3.5 are one construction read once. `τετρααρχέω` as *being tetrarch* and *tetrarch* follows the ASV's own copula.

The `unto` question was the one that needed checking: 3.8 gives *unto Abraham* to the dative name under rule 21, while 3.18 keeps *unto* inside the verb and leaves the article a bare *the*. Not a split - 3.18's object is accusative, and rule 106's accusative arm (with rule 21's own cross-reference to it) decides it that way; 3.14 `Extort from no man` is the same judgment. Recorded as a convention because the competing rule 21 reading is live at 3.18.

BSB: six disagreements, none a genuine error. 3.5 `εἰς` and 3.16 `τῶν`/`αὐτοῦ` are documented convention differences (rules 36, 20); 3.18 `μέν` is rule 70, which says in terms that the report is not a correction; 3.33 `τοῦ` and `Ἀδμίν` are rule 97's mirror case, correctly two `unrepresented` units with the ASV's own note cited. No accepted edge was touched.

Two heads remain genuinely contested and were left as the verse passes decided them, each with a note naming the alternative: `μήποτε` -> *whether haply* headed on *whether* (3.15), and `εὐηγγελίζετο` -> *preached he good tidings unto* headed on *tidings* (3.18).

One reading I could not check against the corpus and so did not promote: 3.16 gives the single English *whose* to the relative `οὗ` and leaves the resumptive `αὐτοῦ` unrepresented. The chapter is consistent in itself and the note records the reverse assignment as the alternative, but the Semitic resumptive recurs elsewhere and deserves corpus evidence before any rule is written for it.
